caveats: These are program facts and screening flags, not eligibility determinations or recommendations. The Tribe decides whether and how to apply.
Program statuses change quickly. Each was read on the date shown on the program's page; confirm with the agency before relying on it.

A match pairs an energy type, ranked from the Tribe's own public planning documents, with programs that name that type or may fit it. It does not say the Tribe is eligible, would be competitive, or should apply.
A type marked possible, confirm with agency is not named in the program's documents.
A forecasted opportunity has no close date; the agency's estimated dates are not deadlines. Opportunity listings come from Grants.gov and state who the agency says may apply.
The ranked energy types are a machine-assisted reading of public planning documents and may be incomplete or out of date. Each Tribe is the authority on its own plans.

cooling_uses.label: Backup power for cooling and critical loads

statuses.open: The agency's page or notice shows the program accepting applications, or operating on a continuing basis, on the date checked.
statuses.closed: The last application window has ended and no new round is open or forecasted.
statuses.forecasted: A future round is announced on the agency's page or Grants.gov but is not open. Estimated dates are not deadlines.
statuses.terminated: The agency has ended the program or its awards by official action.
statuses.enjoined: A court order is holding the program or its funding.
statuses.unknown: No current official page confirms the status.

applicability.applicable: A program document names this use.
applicability.possible, confirm with agency: Plausible from a broader eligible category but not named; confirm with the agency.

programs.name: DOE Office of Indian Energy financial assistance (Unleashing Tribal Energy Development NOFO and earlier rounds)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Indian Energy Policy and Programs
funds: DE-FOA-0003548, Unleashing Tribal Energy Development (posted 2026-03-25): DOE is 'soliciting applications to advance affordable, reliable, and secure energy development of Tribal energy resources for the benefit of Tribes and their members.'

Topic Area 1 projects 'serve the electric loads and support the energy needs of Tribes at the scale of a Tribal community or communities' and 'entail the construction of energy assets and projects.' Topic Area 2 projects 'complete all pre-development activities necessary for the deployment of community scale energy projects.' Topic Area 3 projects 'complete necessary pre-development activities for large scale commercial development of Tribal energy resources.'
Office of Indian Energy: 'provides financial assistance on a competitive basis to develop and deploy energy infrastructure and technology.'

DOE announcement of 2026-10-22: for the first time the Office is 'supporting projects at any phase of development and with a broad set of technologies and approaches'; selected projects include community-scale deployment, predevelopment studies (Tribal utility authorities, transmission and distribution, resource assessments, resiliency measures, workforce development) and planning for large-scale projects, 'including identifying geothermal and other energy resources to supply baseload power, provide resilient backup power.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: Federally recognized Native American Tribal governments and other Native American Tribal organizations (Grants.gov applicant types 07 and 11 on DE-FOA-0003548); the Office serves Indian Tribes and Alaska Native entities.
programs.status_note: Applications for DE-FOA-0003548 closed 2026-07-24 and the Grants.gov listing was archived 2026-08-23. On 2026-10-22 DOE announced over $125 million for 63 Tribe-led projects selected for award negotiations; DOE states that selection is not a commitment to issue an award. The Office's page says it will be updated when new opportunities are available, and no new notice or forecast was found on 2026-10-29.
programs.funding_level: About $50 million expected for the 2026 notice (up to $7.5 million per award, no cost share, 40 awards expected, Grants.gov record). DOE announced over $125 million for 63 selected projects on 2026-10-22. CRS reports $75 million enacted for the Office for FY2026 (P.L. 119-74).
programs.energy_type_note: The notice says projects advance Tribal energy development, 'efficiency, and use'; the 2026-10-22 announcement names geothermal. Other technologies are not named in the pages checked (the approach is described as a 'broad set of technologies'), so every other type is listed as possible. CRS (May 2026) says Congress may consider whether Office funding should support wind and solar, so confirm those with the Office. Projects are on Tribal energy resources; offshore wind and marine energy are listed only because the notice does not exclude them.

cooling_uses.sentence: The 2026-10-22 announcement describes funded studies of 'resiliency measures' and planning that identifies energy resources to 'provide resilient backup power'; whether a future round would pay for backup power equipment is not stated.
Topic Area 1 pays for the 'construction of energy assets and projects' that serve Tribal electric loads; microgrids are not named in the pages checked.

programs.name: DOE Office of Indian Energy Technical Assistance for Tribal Energy Projects
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Indian Energy Policy and Programs
funds: 'Technical assistance for Tribal energy projects is provided at no-cost by experts from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Indian Energy, DOE's national laboratories, and other partnering organizations.'

It 'assists federally recognized Indian Tribes and Tribal entities, including Alaska Native regional corporations and village corporations, with energy planning, energy efficiency assessments, resource assessments, project planning, energy codes and utility formation activities.'

'Energy resilience planning helps determine critical loads for the Tribe in addition to energy project sizing to provide energy resilience.' 'Modeling and analysis technical assistance can include microgrid modeling and assessment, energy resource generation modeling for a specific energy project, and building modeling for energy use and savings.'

Building efficiency assistance 'may include an assessment of heat use in a Tribal building or community and/or a prefeasibility study of other heating options such as waste heat recovery, air source heat pumps, and thermal electric storage systems.' The Office 'cannot advise or facilitate a grant application.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: Federally recognized Indian Tribes and Tribal entities, including Alaska Native regional corporations and village corporations; the page lists the Tribal entities eligible to request assistance.
programs.status_note: Listed as 'Ongoing' on the Office's current opportunities page. Each request is evaluated on its scope and the available budget. This is technical help, not a grant.
programs.energy_type_note: Resource assessments and energy options analysis are described without naming technologies, so generation types are listed as possible.

cooling_uses.sentence: Building efficiency assistance may include a prefeasibility study of air source heat pumps (a study by experts, not equipment funding).
Modeling and analysis assistance can include microgrid modeling and assessment (a study by experts, not construction funding).
Energy resilience planning determines critical loads and sizes energy projects for resilience; backup power is not named.
Building efficiency assessments identify efficiency options for Tribal buildings and homes; weatherization work itself is not funded.

programs.name: Tribal Energy Financing Program (TEFP), formerly the Tribal Energy Loan Guarantee Program (TELGP)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF, formerly the Loan Programs Office)
programs.assistance_listing_note: Not shown on the pages checked.
funds: EDF strategic plan: the Tribal Energy Financing Program (Energy Policy Act of 1992, Section 2602(c)) 'Provides loans or loan guarantees up to $20 billion for energy development projects on Tribal lands.' It supports Tribal energy sovereignty 'through financing of conventional and renewable energy projects, transmission infrastructure, and energy storage systems owned and operated by Tribal entities.'
EDF home page: 'EDF offers financing for: ... Tribal investment in energy-related projects.'

CRS (2026-05-22): section 503 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 'authorized DOE to guarantee up to 90% of a loan (including principal and interest) made to an Indian Tribe or a Tribal energy development organization for energy development.' Guaranteed loans must include a 'subsidy cost' payment, which 'can be paid through appropriations, by the applicant, or a combination thereof.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: An Indian Tribe or a Tribal energy development organization (CRS, citing section 503 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005); the EDF plan describes projects owned and operated by Tribal entities.
programs.status_note: EDF's pre-application page offers 'Request a Pre-Application Consultation for the TEFP Program.' CRS reports the solicitation takes submissions until 2028-08-31, that Public Law 119-21 section 50402 rescinded unobligated Inflation Reduction Act funding and left $10.5 million for the loan subsidy, and that one loan guarantee has been issued ($72.8 million, Viejas Microgrid project) since the first solicitation in 2018.

deadline.what: DOE's last submission date, not a competitive round deadline

checked.quote: The first page of the Solicitation is amended by amending the date for each of (i) “Last Part I Submission Due Date (TELGP)”, (ii) “Last Part II Submission Due Date (TELGP)”, (iii) “Last Part I Submission Due Date (TELP)” and (iv) “Last Part II Submission Due Date (TELP)” to August 31, 2028.

programs.funding_level: Loan authority up to $20 billion (EDF strategic plan). Loan subsidy funding of $10.5 million remains after the rescission, and $6.3 million was appropriated for administrative expenses in FY2026 (CRS, 2026-05-22).
programs.energy_type_note: The EDF plan says 'conventional and renewable energy projects, transmission infrastructure, and energy storage systems'; individual renewable technologies are not listed, so solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal and biomass are read from 'renewable energy projects'. The one guarantee issued financed a microgrid. Confirm current EDF policy on wind and solar with the agency.

cooling_uses.sentence: TEFP finances energy projects and storage owned by Tribal entities, and the one loan guarantee issued so far ($72.8 million) was for the Viejas Microgrid project.
Energy storage systems owned and operated by Tribal entities can be financed; battery backup for cooling or critical loads is not named.

programs.name: High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate (HEEHR) Program for Indian Tribes (Inflation Reduction Act section 50122), with its Administrative and Legal Requirements Document (ALRD)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (Home Energy Rebates Program)
programs.assistance_listing_note: Not shown on the pages checked.
programs.kind: formula grant to Tribes that pays household rebates
funds: 42 U.S.C. 18795a(a)(1)(B): 'to award grants to Indian Tribes to develop and implement a high-efficiency electric home rebate program ... $225,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2031.'

Rebates cover 'not more than $8,000 for a heat pump for space heating or cooling' (42 U.S.C. 18795a(c)(3)). A qualified project includes 'an electric heat pump for space heating and cooling,' insulation, 'air sealing and materials to improve ventilation,' and electric wiring or a load service center.

DOE fact sheet (September 2024): $218.25 million 'in non-competitive formula allocations to Indian Tribes and Alaska Native Corporations'; rebates can cover up to full project cost for low-income households (below 80% of area median income) and up to half for moderate-income households (80 to 150%); an electric heat pump HVAC system is capped at $8,000, with up to $14,000 per dwelling unit in total.

Program Notice 26-3 (effective 2026-05-29): DOE will 'reopen and extend the application deadline'; 'Tribes must apply for their formula awards from the Department by December 11, 2026.' It allows 'rebates for upgrading HVAC and appliances only from existing electric equipment to more efficient electric equipment,' keeps HVAC and appliances in new construction allowable, requires insulation and air sealing before heating and cooling upgrades unless a home is already sealed to a DOE-approved, Tribally specified level, and allows 'dwellings to retain existing fossil-fuel HVAC systems when installing a heat pump.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: Indian Tribes and Alaska Native Corporations apply to DOE for non-competitive formula awards; Tribes can form a consortium or name a third-party agent such as a Tribally designated housing entity. Rebates go to low- and moderate-income households. Program Notice 26-3 also extends low-income categorical eligibility to housing that receives Indian Housing Block Grant funding.
programs.status_note: Program Notice 26-3 reopened the Tribal application period; the deadline is 2026-12-11. DOE's general Home Energy Rebates page says details on active state, territory or Tribal programs are 'coming soon.' Grantees work with their DOE Project Officer. The ALRD (Version 2, 2024-11-07) and the Program Requirements and Application Instructions (Version 2) remain in effect except where the notice changes them.

deadline.what: Tribes must apply to DOE for their formula awards by this date (Program Notice 26-3)

checked.quote: Tribes must apply for their formula awards from the Department by December 11, 2026.

programs.funding_level: $225 million appropriated for Indian Tribes (42 U.S.C. 18795a); about $218.25 million in formula allocations after the 3 percent administrative and technical assistance set-aside (DOE fact sheet).

cooling_uses.sentence: HEEHR section 50122 rebates cover electric heat pumps for space heating and cooling (up to $8,000 per household in the statute), and Program Notice 26-3 lets a dwelling keep an existing fossil-fuel system when installing a heat pump.

Rebates cover insulation, air sealing and ventilation, and Program Notice 26-3 requires them before heating and cooling upgrades unless the home is already sealed to a DOE-approved, Tribally specified level.
Program Notice 26-3 allows HVAC upgrades from existing electric equipment to more efficient electric equipment; cooling-only air conditioners are not named in the sources checked.

programs.name: Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP), including Tribal grantees
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of State and Community Energy Programs
programs.kind: formula grant to states, with direct grants to Tribal organizations by DOE determination
funds: DOE: WAP 'reduces energy costs for low-income households by increasing the energy efficiency of their homes, while ensuring their health and safety.'

42 U.S.C. 6862 and 10 CFR 440.3 list 'cooling efficiency modifications, including, but not limited to, replacement air-conditioners, ventilation equipment, screening, window films, and shading devices,' among weatherization materials, along with insulation, storm windows and doors, and heat-reflective window and door materials.

10 CFR 440.3 also defines a renewable energy system as one that 'transmits or uses solar energy, energy derived from geothermal deposits, energy derived from biomass' for heating or cooling a dwelling, providing hot water or electricity, 'or wind energy for nonbusiness residential purposes.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: 10 CFR 440.11: DOE may grant funds directly to a Tribal organization when it determines that low-income members of an Indian Tribe are not receiving equivalent benefits from the State; otherwise Tribal households are served through the State program (DOE's How to Apply page tells applicants to use the map for their 'state, territory, or Tribe'). Households at or below 200% of the poverty guidelines, or receiving SSI, qualify.
programs.status_note: DOE allocated $325 million in WAP funds and $30 million in Weatherization Readiness Funds to 56 grantees (all states, DC and five territories) on 2025-07-08. The pages checked show no Tribal-specific FY2026 notice, so Tribal access is through state plans or a DOE direct-grant determination.
programs.funding_level: $325 million WAP plus $30 million Weatherization Readiness Funds allocated to 56 state and territory grantees (DOE announcement, 2025-07-08); Tribal shares are set through state plans or direct grants.
programs.energy_type_note: 10 CFR 440.3 defines renewable energy systems for dwellings (solar, geothermal, biomass, residential wind); whether a grantee funds them varies, so they are listed as possible.

cooling_uses.sentence: WAP pays for 'cooling efficiency modifications' that include replacement air conditioners, ventilation equipment, screening, window films and shading devices (42 U.S.C. 6862; 10 CFR 440.3), in income-eligible homes.
WAP is the federal weatherization program: insulation, storm windows and doors, heat-reflective window and door materials and other efficiency measures for income-eligible homes.

Heat pumps are not named in the sources checked; replacement of heating or cooling equipment is allowed as a cooling efficiency modification or an energy conserving device under 'such other' measures.
The list of cooling efficiency modifications is 'including, but not limited to,' so evaporative coolers could qualify; they are not named.
Roof coatings are not named; heat-reflective window and door materials and shading devices are named.

programs.name: Grid Resilience State and Tribal Formula Grants (Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act section 40101(d))
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Electricity (with the National Energy Technology Laboratory)
programs.assistance_listing_note: Not shown on the pages checked.
funds: DOE: the program 'is designed to strengthen and modernize America's power grid against wildfires, severe storms, and other natural disasters' and 'will distribute funding to states, territories, and federally recognized Indian Tribes, including Alaska Native Regional Corporations and Alaska Native Village Corporations, over five years based on a formula.'

42 U.S.C. 18711(e)(1): grants may be used for 'activities, technologies, equipment, and hardening measures to reduce the likelihood and consequences of disruptive events, including ... the use or construction of distributed energy resources for enhancing system adaptive capacity during disruptive events, including (i) microgrids; and (ii) battery-storage subcomponents.' The list also names monitoring and control technologies, undergrounding, and power line hardening. ('Weatherization technologies and equipment' in that list means hardening grid equipment against weather, not home weatherization.)

Grants may not be used to build a new electric generating facility, or a large-scale battery storage facility that is not used for enhancing system adaptive capacity during disruptive events (42 U.S.C. 18711(e)(2)). Each Tribe must match 15 percent of its grant.
programs.tribal_eligibility: Federally recognized Indian Tribes, including Alaska Native Regional Corporations and Alaska Native Village Corporations; each Tribe submits an application with a plan adopted after notice and a public hearing (42 U.S.C. 18711(d)).
programs.status_note: DOE issued Amendment 10 of the ALRD on 2026-10-20, opening a 120-day application period for FY25-FY26 funds (Years 4 and 5 of the 5-year program) for existing grant recipients and new applicants.

checked.quote: The FY25-FY26 application deadline will be February 17, 2027 at 11:59pm EST.

programs.funding_level: FY25 and FY26 allocations combined total $967,104,372 across all eligible applicants; DOE's allocation table lists each Tribe's amount.
programs.energy_type_note: Solar can be part of a distributed energy resource used for adaptive capacity, but the statute bars new generating facilities as such.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays for battery-storage subcomponents and other distributed energy resources that add adaptive capacity during outages (42 U.S.C. 18711(e)); DOE's page links a guide to installing back-up battery power systems on Tribal facilities.
Microgrids are named as an eligible use for enhancing system adaptive capacity during disruptive events (42 U.S.C. 18711(e)(1)).

programs.name: Energy Improvements in Rural or Remote Areas (ERA)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations
funds: DOE: the program 'gives communities with 10,000 or fewer people the tools and resources they need to improve the resilience, reliability, and affordability of their local energy systems.'

FY2025 notice DE-FOA-0003428: applicants 'must propose projects that support at least one of these eligible activities: A. Improving overall cost-effectiveness of energy generation, transmission, or distribution systems; B. Siting or upgrading transmission and distribution lines; C. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from energy generation in rural or remote areas; D. Providing or modernizing electric generation facilities; E. Developing microgrids; and F. Increasing energy efficiency.' 'Applications may include any technology that meets these eligible activities, as long as those technologies are commercially available.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: The Grants.gov record lists applicant type 'Unrestricted' (open to any type of entity) for communities of 10,000 people or fewer. Tribal eligibility is not separately stated in the records checked.
programs.status_note: DE-FOA-0003428 (FY2025 release) closed 2025-08-28 and was archived 2025-09-27. The program page lists no newer notice. DOE announced on 2025-10-01 the termination of 321 awards (223 projects) from several offices, including the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations; the announcement does not name this program.
programs.funding_level: About $400 million expected for the FY2025 release (award ceiling $50 million, cost share required).
programs.sources_note: The list of eligible activities is quoted from the opportunity description the Grants.gov API returns (fetchOpportunity, opportunity 356630); the simpler.grants.gov page shows a shortened description.
programs.energy_type_note: The notice accepts 'any technology that meets these eligible activities' (modernizing electric generation, microgrids, efficiency), so generation types are possible.

cooling_uses.sentence: The FY2025 notice names 'developing microgrids' as an eligible activity; no round is open now.
'Increasing energy efficiency' is an eligible activity; weatherization is not named.

programs.name: Community Microgrid Assistance Partnership (C-MAP)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Electricity
funds: The program 'provides funding and technical assistance to energy providers and partners to build, operate, and enhance microgrid systems that improve the affordability, reliability, and security of electricity in remote areas of the United States.'

'C-MAP issues periodic requests for funding proposals and offers on-demand, short-term Microgrid Support Services that range from brief, high-level guidance sessions to as many as sixty hours of tailored technical support from national laboratory subject-matter experts.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: 'Eligible applicants include nonprofit organizations such as energy cooperatives, industry, state and local governments, and federally recognized American Indian and Alaska Native Tribes and villages.'
programs.status_note: The page says the latest C-MAP 2026 funding opportunity 'is now closed' and awardees will be announced in Fall 2026. The page also invites applications for on-demand Microgrid Support Services (news item dated 2026-05-20), so the technical assistance side is still accepting requests.
programs.funding_level: Up to $3.5 million available for the 2026 round (page news item dated 2026-05-12).
programs.geography: Remote areas of the United States
programs.energy_type_note: The page describes microgrid systems in general; generation and storage components are not itemized.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays for, and gives technical help on, building, operating and enhancing microgrid systems in remote areas (the 2026 funding round is closed; support services accept requests).
Microgrids that keep power on during outages could carry cooling loads; backup power for cooling is not named.

programs.name: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), including Tribal grantees
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Administration for Children and Families, Office of Community Services
programs.assistance_listing_note: Not shown on the pages checked; this is the number HHS publishes for LIHEAP. Confirm on SAM.gov.
programs.kind: block grant (formula) to states, Tribes and territories
funds: ACF: 'LIHEAP provides federally funded assistance to reduce the costs associated with home energy bills, energy crises, weatherization, and minor energy-related home repairs. LIHEAP can help you stay warm in the winter and cool in the summer through programs that reduce the risk of health and safety problems that arise from unsafe heating and cooling situations and practices.'

42 U.S.C. 8622(6): 'The term home energy means a source of heating or cooling in residential dwellings.' Grantees assist low-income households with home energy costs, 'intervene in energy crisis situations' and 'provide low-cost residential weatherization and other cost-effective energy-related home repair' (42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(1)).

The LIHEAP Clearinghouse tells Tribal grantees to plan spending for each type of assistance (heating, cooling, crisis or weatherization) and publishes Tribal benefit levels for heating, cooling and crisis.
programs.tribal_eligibility: Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations receive LIHEAP grants directly when the Secretary determines that Tribal members would be better served by direct grants (42 U.S.C. 8623(d)); ACF publishes allocation tables for Tribal grant recipients. Assistance goes to low-income households through the Tribal LIHEAP office; LIHEAP does not give direct grants to individuals.
programs.status_note: On 2026-10-09 ACF announced the first FY2027 funding release: about $3.6 billion of regular block grant funds released to all LIHEAP grantees, equal to 90 percent of funds under the continuing resolution (Public Law 119-103, signed 2026-09-02), allocated by the annual formula update. Grantees need an approved FY2027 Model Plan to draw funds.
programs.funding_level: About $3.6 billion of FY2027 regular block grant funds released to all grantees on 2026-10-09; Tribal amounts are in ACF's allocation tables.
programs.energy_type_note: Weatherization and minor energy-related home repair are named; equipment replacement depends on each grantee's plan.

cooling_uses.sentence: LIHEAP can pay for low-cost residential weatherization and other cost-effective energy-related home repair (42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(1)), at the grantee's option within its plan.

LIHEAP covers 'home energy,' defined as heating or cooling, and Tribal plans set cooling benefit levels; whether a given Tribal plan pays for buying or repairing air conditioners or fans varies by plan.

programs.name: Indian Housing Block Grant (IHBG), formula and competitive (IHBG-COMP)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Native American Programs
programs.kind: formula grant, plus a competitive grant program
funds: HUD: 'It is a formula grant that is distributed annually and funds affordable housing activities including new housing construction, rehabilitation, and housing services, and much more.'

25 U.S.C. 4132(2), development: 'The acquisition, new construction, reconstruction, or moderate or substantial rehabilitation of affordable housing, which may include real property acquisition, site improvement, development and rehabilitation of utilities, necessary infrastructure, and utility services, conversion, demolition, financing, administration and planning, improvement to achieve greater energy efficiency, mold remediation, and other related activities.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: 'Eligible IHBG recipients are federally recognized Tribes, Tribally Designated Housing Entities (TDHEs), and a limited number of State-recognized Tribes.' Each year recipients submit an Indian Housing Plan.
programs.status_note: The formula grant is distributed every year through each recipient's Indian Housing Plan. The competitive IHBG-COMP notice for FY2026 (PIH-2600-DC-0048) is forecasted on Grants.gov (forecast dated 2026-06-08, about $125 million, up to 30 awards); the FY2025 IHBG-COMP closed 2026-01-15.
programs.energy_type_note: Energy efficiency improvements are named in the statute; heat pumps or solar in new or rehabilitated housing would be housing development costs but are not named.

cooling_uses.sentence: IHBG pays for 'improvement to achieve greater energy efficiency' as part of developing, building or rehabilitating affordable housing (25 U.S.C. 4132(2)).
Rehabilitation and new construction of Tribal housing can include cooling equipment; air conditioners are not named in the statute or on HUD's page.
Heat pump installation would be a rehabilitation or new construction cost; it is not named.

programs.name: Indian Community Development Block Grant (ICDBG), single purpose and imminent threat
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Native American Programs
programs.kind: competitive grant, plus noncompetitive imminent threat grants
funds: HUD: ICDBG 'provides eligible grantees with direct grants for use in developing viable Indian and Alaska Native Communities, including decent housing, a suitable living environment, and economic opportunities, primarily for low and moderate income persons.'

Categories: 'Housing rehabilitation, land acquisition to support new housing construction, and under limited circumstances, new housing construction'; community facilities, meaning 'Infrastructure construction, e.g., roads, water and sewer facilities; and, single or multipurpose community buildings'; and economic development.

Imminent threat grants: the Secretary may set aside 'up to $5 million of each year's allocation for the noncompetitive, first come-first served, funding of grants to eliminate or lessen problems which pose an imminent threat to public health or safety of Tribal residents.'
24 CFR 1003.201(c), public facilities and improvements: 'design features and improvements which promote energy efficiency may be included.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: 'Any Indian Tribe, band, group, or nation (including Alaska Indians, Aleut, and Eskimos) or Alaska Native village which has established a relationship to the Federal government as defined in the program regulations. In certain instances, Tribal organizations may be eligible to apply.'
programs.status_note: Two FY2026 ICDBG notices are forecasted on Grants.gov (PIH-2600-DC-0034, forecast dated 2026-05-18, and PIH-2600-DC-0023, forecast dated 2026-10-06; about $90 million estimated in each, Tribal governments listed as eligible). The FY2025 notice closed 2025-12-10. HUD's page lists ICDBG imminent threat technical assistance from 2026-07-09; the imminent threat application instructions (FR-6900-N-74) show a 2026-09-30 close on Grants.gov. A forecast's estimated dates are not deadlines.
programs.funding_level: About $90 million estimated in each FY2026 forecast (Grants.gov); up to $5 million per year may be set aside for imminent threat grants (HUD).
programs.energy_type_note: Energy efficiency features in public facilities are named in 24 CFR 1003.201(c); renewable generation or heat pumps are not named.

cooling_uses.sentence: ICDBG pays for 'single or multipurpose community buildings' and public facilities; a building used as a cooling center fits that category but cooling centers are not named.
Housing rehabilitation and community building construction can include cooling equipment; air conditioners are not named.
Housing rehabilitation is an eligible category and energy efficiency design features may be included in public facilities; weatherization is not named.
Imminent threat grants address 'an imminent threat to public health or safety'; whether a heat emergency or power outage qualifies, and whether generators are eligible, is not stated.

programs.name: FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Federal Emergency Management Agency
programs.assistance_listing_note: As recorded from the FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance Guide in the TCR registry; Grants.gov lists no notices under this number.
funds: FEMA: HMGP 'provides funding to state, local, Tribal and territorial governments to develop hazard mitigation plans and rebuild in ways that reduce or mitigate future disaster losses in their communities. This funding becomes available following a Presidentially declared disaster.' Eligible projects include 'Retrofitting buildings to make them more resistant to floods, earthquakes, wind, wildfires and other natural hazards' and 'Upgrading utilities and infrastructure to enhance resistance to natural hazards.'

FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance Program and Policy Guide (March 23, 2023), as quoted in the TCR registry: D.2.11, 'The purchase and installation of secondary power sources and related equipment, such as generators, microgrids, solar photovoltaic systems, and battery back-up systems are generally eligible if they are cost-effective'; B.11.2.3, 'Microgrids are eligible under HMGP, HMGP Post Fire and BRIC. Unlike generators or solar photovoltaic secondary power sources, microgrids are not limited to critical facilities.' Part 12 lists, for extreme heat, nature-based solutions such as green roofs and increased tree canopy.
programs.tribal_eligibility: FEMA: state, local, Tribal and territorial governments, each with an adopted hazard mitigation plan. HMA Guide B.4 (as quoted in the TCR registry): 'A federally recognized Tribal government has the option to apply for the HMA programs through the state as a subapplicant (when permitted) or directly to FEMA as an applicant.'
programs.status_note: Conditional: funding becomes available only after a Presidentially declared disaster. FEMA's page directs prospective applicants to their State, Tribe or territory hazard mitigation office. The TCR registry reports that FEMA's extreme-heat guidance pages returned 'This file is unpublished' on 2026-10-29; that was not re-checked here.
programs.sources_note: FEMA blocks automated download of the Guide, so its wording is carried from the TCR registry and was not re-read on 2026-10-29. The program page was read on that date.
programs.energy_type_note: Solar photovoltaic systems and battery back-up systems are eligible as secondary power sources; generators and solar are limited to critical facilities, microgrids are not.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays for secondary power sources and related equipment, such as generators, solar photovoltaic systems and battery back-up systems, if cost-effective (HMA Guide D.2.11, quoted in the TCR registry); generators and solar are limited to critical facilities.
Microgrids are eligible under HMGP and, unlike generators or solar, are not limited to critical facilities (HMA Guide B.11.2.3, quoted in the TCR registry).
The Guide names green roofs and tree canopy for extreme heat and climate-smart building materials that 'reduce or help withstand extreme temperatures'; cool roofs are not named.

Retrofitting a public building or backing it up with secondary power could serve a cooling center; the TCR registry reports FEMA's cooling center guidance was unpublished, and cooling centers are not named on the program page.
Retrofits for extreme temperatures are described, but cooling systems for public buildings are not named in the sources re-read.

programs.name: FEMA Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Federal Emergency Management Agency
funds: FEMA: BRIC 'provides federal funding to states, U.S. territories, federally recognized Tribal Nations, and local governments for pre-disaster hazard mitigation activities that strengthen infrastructure, reduce risks from natural hazards, and build long-term resilience.'

FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance Guide (March 23, 2023), as quoted in the TCR registry: 'Microgrids are eligible under HMGP, HMGP Post Fire and BRIC' and secondary power sources, including generators, microgrids, solar photovoltaic systems and battery back-up systems, are generally eligible if cost-effective.
programs.tribal_eligibility: Federally recognized Tribal Nations (FEMA BRIC page); an approved hazard mitigation plan is required (TCR registry, HMA Guide B.4).
programs.status_note: FEMA's page says the application period for the Fiscal Years 2024 and 2025 BRIC annual grant cycle is closed; subapplications were due 3 p.m. ET on July 23, 2026. FEMA is reviewing submissions and will announce selections afterward. Subapplications for the January 2025 funding opportunity 'will not be reviewed.'
programs.funding_level: $1 billion made available for the FY2024-25 cycle (published 2026-03-25).
programs.sources_note: The Guide wording is carried from the TCR registry (FEMA blocks automated download). The program page was read on 2026-10-29.
programs.energy_type_note: Same secondary power wording as HMGP.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays for secondary power sources and related equipment, including generators, solar photovoltaic systems and battery back-up systems, if cost-effective (HMA Guide D.2.11, quoted in the TCR registry); the FY2024-25 round is closed.
Microgrids are eligible under BRIC (HMA Guide B.11.2.3, quoted in the TCR registry); the FY2024-25 round is closed.
Green roofs and tree canopy are named for extreme heat; cool roofs are not named.
Strengthening a public building so it can serve as a cooling center fits pre-disaster mitigation of infrastructure; cooling centers are not named.

programs.name: Climate Pollution Reduction Grants (CPRG) Implementation Grants, Tribes and Territories Competition
programs.agency: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
programs.kind: competitive grant (competition complete; selected applicants only)
funds: EPA: 'announced 34 selected applications for $300 million in grants to Tribes and one U.S. territory to implement community-driven solutions to tackle the climate crisis, reduce air pollution, and accelerate the clean energy transition.'

Anticipated results from the selected applications include 'Installation of 34 megawatts of solar and wind power generation capacity and deployment of 27 megawatt-hours of battery storage capacity,' 'Installation of solar panels on more than 800 homes and 4 municipal buildings,' and 'Deployment of an estimated 1,875 heat pumps in residences and public buildings.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: Tribal governments applied; the selected applications are from 33 Tribal recipients and the Municipality of Saipan.
programs.status_note: The competition closed (Grants.gov EPA-R-OAR-CPRGT-23-09 closed 2024-05-01 and is archived); no new round is listed. EPA's CPRG page (last updated 2025-11-26) says EPA 'is working to award' the $300 million to the 34 selected applications, and the selections page (last updated 2026-08-12) states no award or termination status. Selected Tribes should confirm award status with EPA.
programs.funding_level: $300 million estimated for the 34 selected applications.
programs.energy_type_note: Types are those the selected applications describe (solar, wind, battery storage, heat pumps and electric vehicle chargers, efficiency audits and improvements); the competition is closed, so these show what was funded, not what is open.

cooling_uses.sentence: Selected applications include 'deployment of an estimated 1,875 heat pumps in residences and public buildings'; this shows what the competition funded and no new round is open.
Selected applications include audits and energy efficiency improvements for over 1,000 residences; the competition is closed.

programs.name: USDA High Energy Cost Grants
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Rural Development, Rural Utilities Service
funds: USDA: the program 'assists energy providers and other eligible entities in lowering energy costs for families and individuals in communities with extremely high per-household energy costs (275 percent of the national average or higher).'

Funds finance 'the acquisition, construction or improvement of facilities serving eligible communities,' including 'Electric generation, transmission and distribution facilities'; 'Renewable energy facilities, including solar, wind, hydropower or biomass technologies used for on- or off-grid: electric power generation, water or space heating, process heating and power'; 'Backup or emergency power generation or energy storage technology, including generation equipment installed on consumer premises'; and 'Energy efficiency improvements and conservation measures (i.e. weatherization of residences and community facilities).'
programs.tribal_eligibility: 'Most retail or power supply providers serving an eligible rural community, including ... Federally-recognized Tribes and Tribal entities.' The community's average household energy cost must exceed 275 percent of the national average under the benchmarks in the 2025 funding announcement.
programs.status_note: USDA's page shows 'Application Window: CLOSED' and 'No competition is planned for FY2026.' Grants.gov lists the FY2025 notice (RD-RUS-HECG25) as archived.
programs.geography: Rural communities with household energy costs above 275 percent of the national average
programs.energy_type_note: Storage is read from 'backup or emergency power generation or energy storage technology.' Microgrids and geothermal are not named.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays for 'backup or emergency power generation or energy storage technology, including generation equipment installed on consumer premises' (no round is planned for FY2026).
Pays for energy efficiency and conservation measures, 'i.e. weatherization of residences and community facilities' (no round is planned for FY2026).
Electric generation, transmission and distribution facilities and storage are eligible; microgrids are not named.

programs.name: Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) Renewable Energy Systems and Energy Efficiency Improvement Grants (guaranteed loans also available)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Rural Development
funds: USDA: 'The program competitively awards grant money to agricultural producers and rural small businesses to reimburse expenses for the installation of renewable energy systems or energy efficiency improvement projects.'

Renewable energy systems: biomass (biodiesel and ethanol, anaerobic digesters, solid fuel), geothermal for electricity or direct use, hydropower under 30 megawatts, hydrogen, wind turbines, solar, and ocean energy 'that use tides, currents or thermal energy.' Efficiency: 'High-efficiency heating, cooling, and ventilation (HVAC) systems,' insulation, lighting, 'High-efficiency cooling or refrigeration units,' and energy-efficient doors and windows.

Grants cover up to 25 percent of project costs ($1,500 minimum; $500,000 maximum for renewable energy systems and $250,000 for efficiency). The project must be in a rural area of 50,000 residents or less, and 'Beginning October 16, 2026, all solar pv and wind projects cannot include components made in countries designated as foreign adversaries.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: Rural agricultural producers and rural small businesses, including 'A business that is wholly owned by an Indian Tribe.' A Tribal government itself is not named; a Tribe's wholly owned business must be an existing business and the highest-level owner of the project.
programs.status_note: USDA's page shows 'Application Window: CLOSED': 'The Agency is not accepting REAP grant applications at this time. A Notice of Funding Opportunity identifying the application period will publish soon. Guaranteed loan applications may be submitted.' Grants.gov lists the FY2025 notice (RDBCP-REAP-RES-EEI-2025) as archived.
programs.funding_level: Grants up to 25 percent of project costs, $1,500 to $500,000 (renewable energy) or $250,000 (efficiency); guaranteed loans may bring total REAP funding to 75 percent of costs.
programs.geography: Rural areas with populations of 50,000 or less
programs.energy_type_note: Tribal governments are not named as applicants, only businesses wholly owned by a Tribe; storage and microgrids are not named.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays 25 percent of the cost of 'high-efficiency heating, cooling, and ventilation (HVAC) systems' and 'high-efficiency cooling or refrigeration units' for a Tribe-owned rural business (grants are closed now; guaranteed loans are open).
Pays for insulation and energy-efficient doors and windows for a Tribe-owned rural business (grants are closed now).
Heat pumps are a form of high-efficiency HVAC but are not named on the page.

programs.status_label: closed for grants; guaranteed loans open

programs.name: USDA Community Facilities Direct Loan and Grant Program
programs.agency: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Rural Development
programs.assistance_listing_note: Number as listed for Community Facilities opportunities on Grants.gov; not shown on the program page.
funds: USDA: 'This program provides affordable funding to develop essential community facilities in rural areas.' 'Funds can be used to purchase, construct, and / or improve essential community facilities, purchase equipment and pay related project expenses.'

Examples include 'community centers,' health care facilities, public safety buildings and equipment, and public facilities. Grants cover up to 75, 55, 35 or 15 percent of costs depending on community size and income.
programs.tribal_eligibility: 'Eligible borrowers include: Public bodies; Community-based non-profit corporations; Federally Recognized Tribes.' Rural areas, including Federally Recognized Tribal Lands, with no more than 20,000 residents.
programs.status_note: USDA's page shows 'Application Window: OPEN'; applications are accepted on an ongoing basis from October 1 through September 30, subject to funds.
programs.geography: Rural areas with no more than 20,000 residents, including Federally Recognized Tribal Lands
programs.energy_type_note: This is not an energy program; it pays for community buildings and equipment, so it is used only in the cooling and heat listing.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays to build or improve essential community facilities such as community centers and to buy equipment; a cooling center is not named.
Improvement of an essential community facility and 'equipment' purchases could include cooling systems; air conditioners are not named.
Public safety equipment and facility improvements are eligible; generators for a community facility are not named.

programs.name: BIA Energy and Mineral Development Program (EMDP) grants
programs.agency: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs, Division of Energy and Mineral Development
funds: FY2026 notice BIA-EMDP-2026: 'The EMDP grant seeks to identify, evaluate, and assess, energy or mineral resources and related projects on Indian land.'
'EMDP grants may only fund projects occurring on Indian land' as defined in 25 U.S.C. 3501.
programs.tribal_eligibility: 'Only Indian Tribes and Tribal Energy Development Organizations (TEDOs) are eligible to receive EMDP grants for projects on Indian land' (Energy Policy Act of 2005, 25 U.S.C. 3501-3503).
programs.status_note: The FY2026 notice closed 2026-06-18 and the Grants.gov listing was archived 2026-06-30. The FY2025 notice ran 2025-07-01 to 2025-08-13, so rounds recur annually, but no FY2027 forecast was found on 2026-10-29.
programs.funding_level: $7.4 million expected for FY2026 (up to $2.5 million per award, about 20 awards, no cost share).
programs.energy_type_note: The notice covers 'energy or mineral resources' without naming technologies, so resource types on Indian land are listed as possible. It is the BIA's resource assessment and feasibility grant.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays to identify, evaluate and assess energy resources and 'related projects' on Indian land, which could include a microgrid feasibility study; microgrids are not named.

programs.name: BIA Tribal Electrification Program (TEP)
programs.agency: U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Assistant Secretary - Indian Affairs (with the Bureau of Indian Affairs)
programs.assistance_listing_note: Not shown on the pages checked.
funds: BIA: 'The Tribal Electrification Program (TEP) will utilize $145.5 million to increase the number of Tribal homes with reliable and efficient electricity,' with $4.5 million for technical assistance; the program was allocated $150 million through the Inflation Reduction Act.

Round 2 guidance, permissible uses: '1. the provision of electricity to unelectrified Tribal homes through zero-emissions energy systems. 2. transitioning electrified Tribal homes to zero-emissions energy systems; and 3. associated home repairs and retrofitting necessary to install the zero-emissions energy systems.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: 'Eligibility is limited to Federally recognized Indian Tribes and Tribal Organizations authorized by Indian Tribal governments,' Tribal coalitions, and Tribal entities (Round 2 guidance).
programs.status_note: BIA's page, under 'Round 1 and 2 Completion,' says selections for the final awards were publicly announced in September 2024. An archived Interior release (2024-03-05) reported the first round: $72 million to 21 Tribes. No open round was found on 2026-10-29.
programs.funding_level: $150 million allocated through the Inflation Reduction Act ($145.5 million for awards).
programs.energy_type_note: The guidance says 'zero-emissions energy systems' without naming technologies, so they are listed as possible. The program is for homes, not community buildings.

cooling_uses.sentence: Pays for zero-emissions energy systems and home retrofits that electrify Tribal homes; microgrids are not named and the rounds are complete.

programs.name: Elective pay (direct pay) for clean energy tax credits, Internal Revenue Code section 6417, as changed by Public Law 119-21
programs.agency: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Internal Revenue Service
programs.assistance_listing_note: A tax provision, not a grant program.
programs.kind: tax credit paid as a refund to the Tribal government
funds: IRS: 'Elective pay makes certain clean energy tax credits ... effectively refundable ... The entity can receive the full value of the credit because the IRS treats the elective payment amount as a tax payment. We then count it as overpayment on the return and refund it to the entity.'

IRS Publication 5817-G describes the Clean Electricity Investment Credit (section 48E) as a 'technology-neutral tax credit for investment in facilities that generate clean electricity and qualified energy storage technologies,' at 6 percent of qualified investment or 30 percent if prevailing wage and apprenticeship rules are met. For credits before 2025 it lists section 45 'wind, biomass, geothermal, solar, small irrigation, landfill and trash, hydropower, marine and hydrokinetic energy' and section 48 'fuel cell, solar, geothermal, small wind, energy storage, biogas, microgrid controllers, and combined heat and power.'

Public Law 119-21: sections 45Y and 48E end for 'an applicable wind facility or applicable solar facility that is placed in service after December 31, 2027'; the termination applies to wind and solar 'the construction of which begins after July 4, 2026' (IRS Notice 2025-42). The 45W commercial clean vehicle credit 'will not be allowed for any vehicle acquired after Sept. 30, 2025' (IRS).
programs.tribal_eligibility: IRS FAQ Q4: 'An Indian Tribal government, subdivision thereof, or any agency or instrumentality of a Tribal government or political subdivision is eligible for elective pay.' The December 2025 final rule (TD 10039, effective 2026-01-15) treats entities wholly owned by Tribes as instrumentalities for elective pay. The entity must register with the IRS before filing.
programs.status_note: Elective pay remains available to Tribal governments, but Public Law 119-21 changed what it pays for. The July 4, 2026 construction-start date for wind and solar has passed, so a new wind or solar project that has not begun construction must be placed in service by 2027-12-31. The beginning-of-construction rules in Notice 2025-42 may have changed after a court decision reported in June 2026; that was not confirmed on an official page, so confirm current rules with the IRS or a tax advisor.
programs.funding_level: Credit value of 6 percent of qualified investment, or 30 percent with prevailing wage and apprenticeship compliance, with bonuses for energy communities and domestic content (Publication 5817-G; FAQ).
programs.energy_type_note: Section 48E names qualified facilities and energy storage technology and ends for wind and solar placed in service after 2027. Publication 5817-G names the other technologies only for the pre-2025 credits (sections 45 and 48) and calls sections 45Y and 48E technology-neutral, so they are listed as possible; confirm a facility's eligibility with a tax advisor.

cooling_uses.sentence: Energy storage technology qualifies for the section 48E investment credit, so a battery system that backs up cooling loads can earn the credit if it meets the credit's rules; backup power is not named.
Publication 5817-G lists microgrid controllers as section 48 property for pre-2025 construction; whether a microgrid's components qualify under 48E depends on the components.

programs.name: Bureau of Reclamation WaterSMART Water and Energy Efficiency Grants
programs.agency: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Reclamation
funds: Reclamation 'provides 50/50 cost share funding to irrigation and water districts, Tribes, states and other entities with water or power delivery authority. Projects conserve and use water more efficiently; increase the production of hydropower; mitigate conflict risk in areas at a high risk of future water conflict; and accomplish other benefits that contribute to water supply reliability in the western United States.'
programs.tribal_eligibility: Tribes are named among eligible entities: 'irrigation and water districts, Tribes, states and other entities with water or power delivery authority' in the western United States.
programs.status_note: 'The FY25 Water and Energy Efficiency Grants funding opportunity selections were announced June 3, 2026' (31 projects, $38.9 million). Grants.gov lists the FY2024 notice (R24AS00052) as closed, and no FY2026 notice of this grant was posted or forecasted on 2026-10-29.
programs.funding_level: $38.9 million awarded to 31 projects in the FY25 round.
programs.energy_type_note: Hydropower within water delivery systems.

programs.name: BPA Tribal Income Qualified Energy Conservation Grants
programs.agency: Bonneville Power Administration
funds: BPA: 'BPA offers income qualified (IQ) energy conservation direct and non-competitive grants to Tribal governments. Tribal IQ grants fund the same energy efficiency technologies as the state grant program, but funds are allocated directly to the Tribe in a government-to-government partnership.'

'Funding for the Tribal IQ grant program budget is approximately $600,000 per year and is negotiated annually.' Homes must be occupied by a member of a federally recognized Tribe, receive electricity from a BPA customer utility, and have electric heat as the primary heat source for most measures.
programs.tribal_eligibility: Tribal governments across BPA's service territory; households must be income qualified (Tribes may follow general guidelines or set their own with BPA approval).
programs.status_note: 'Grant applications are now being accepted for fiscal year 2027.' Priority application due date 2026-10-01; 'November 5, 2026 and Beyond: Application due date to ensure funding is available, but applications will be accepted throughout the year as funding is available.'

deadline.what: Application due date to ensure funding is available; later applications accepted while funds last

checked.quote: November 5, 2026 and Beyond: Application due date to ensure funding is available, but applications will be accepted throughout the year as funding is available.

programs.geography: BPA service territory (Pacific Northwest); homes must be served by a BPA customer utility
programs.energy_type_note: The page says the grants fund the same energy efficiency technologies as the state program without listing them.

cooling_uses.sentence: Energy conservation upgrades for Tribal member homes with electric heat are funded; the measure list is in BPA's grant scope of work, not on the page read.
Efficient heating and cooling equipment may be among the funded measures; heat pumps are not named on the page read.
